text: {"answer": "A zeta potential near zero means the electrostatic charge on particle surfaces is minimal, so the repulsive forces that normally keep particles apart are greatly reduced (PMC10313666:L27, PMC13488408:L23). Without sufficient repulsion, the attractive forces (e.g., van der Waals) between particles dominate, allowing particles to collide and stick together, i.e., aggregate (PMC10313666:L27, PMC8617854:L34). This zero-charge condition, sometimes called the isoelectric point, is specifically associated with a loss of colloidal stability and increased tendency to agglomerate, whereas high positive or negative zeta potentials (e.g., beyond ±30 mV) confer strong repulsion and stability (PMC11494166:L27, PMC12003597:L64, PMC10260929:L35).", "citations": ["PMC10313666:L27", "PMC8617854:L34", "PMC13488408:L23", "PMC11494166:L27", "PMC12003597:L64", "PMC10260929:L35"]}

{"answer": "Divalent cations like Ca2+ are far more effective at destabilizing plastic-particle suspensions because the critical coagulation concentration is inversely proportional to the sixth power of ionic charge, making divalent ions 50–83 times more influential than monovalent ions (PMC12376886:L46). Mechanistically, Ca2+ produces stronger charge neutralization and screening of the particles' negative surface charge than Na+, compressing the electric double layer and reducing electrostatic repulsion more effectively (PMC11899741:L77; PMC9142603:L85; PMC13213765:L44). This charge screening/neutralization by divalent ions is stronger than by monovalent ions at the same ionic strength because of their higher charge, and can also involve cation bridging between particles, both of which promote aggregation and retention/adsorption of the particles (PMC11899741:L77; PMC11543686:L77).", "citations": ["PMC12376886:L46", "PMC11899741:L77", "PMC9142603:L85", "PMC13213765:L44", "PMC11543686:L77"]}

{"answer": "The eco-corona/biofilm coats the bare plastic surface with biomolecules (proteins, humic/fulvic acids, amino acids, lipids, polysaccharides, EPS), effectively replacing the original polymer surface with a new charged layer, so the measured zeta potential reflects this coating rather than the pristine plastic (PMC10830523:L132; PMC13057466:L19). Molecules such as humic and fulvic acids carry multiple carboxylic groups that add negative charge, and different densities/types of charged sites on the corona alter electrostatic interactions, making environmentally exposed particles more negative than pristine ones (PMC10830523:L132, L134). The specific composition of the corona matters: EPS or eco-corona adsorption can leave anionic (bare/COOH) particle charge largely unchanged while strongly reducing or even reversing the positive charge of aminated particles, especially with high-molecular-weight EPS, because the adsorbed layer's own functional groups (e.g., carboxyl/amine) and its physical properties (adsorbed mass, thickness) determine the net surface charge (PMC13057466:L43, L47). Similarly, adsorption of soil metabolites onto microplastics increases zeta potential by altering surface functional-group composition and charge distribution as the corona forms (PMC13394419:L25, L31). A robust, thick hard corona layer can also shield the underlying particle's intrinsic charge, further lowering the measured zeta potential magnitude (PMC4958399:L42)."}

{"answer": "Increasing ionic strength adds more electrolyte ions that screen (compress) the electrical double layer surrounding a charged particle, an effect described as electrostatic screening or charge screening by the background ions. This compression of the double layer reduces the electrokinetic response measured at the slipping plane, lowering the magnitude of the zeta potential even though the underlying particle charge/interaction mechanisms remain the same. Correspondingly, at low ionic strength the double layer is less compressed, which maximizes zeta potential magnitude and sensitivity to interaction-induced changes.", "citations": ["PMC13298883:L15", "PMC13298883:L10", "PMC9142603:L85"]}

{"answer": "Carboxyl and amine surface functionalisation add different ionizable chemical groups to the polymer particle surface, and these groups carry opposite charges depending on their protonation state: carboxyl (-COOH) groups deprotonate to form negatively charged carboxylate groups, while amine (-NH2) groups can be protonated to form positively charged -NH3+ groups. However, whether the amine group is actually positively charged depends on solution pH relative to the amine's pKa; if pH is below the pKa, protonation is limited, which combined with the inherent negative charge of the polystyrene core itself can result in amine-functionalised particles still showing a net negative zeta potential rather than the theoretically expected positive charge.", "citations": ["PMC13104249:L17", "PMC12890322:L35"]}

{"answer": "Natural organic matter (NOM)—including humic/fulvic acids and related substances—adsorbs onto particle surfaces, forming an eco-corona that introduces its own charged functional groups (e.g., multiple carboxylic groups on humic/fulvic acids), thereby altering the measured zeta potential rather than the bare plastic surface itself (PMC10830523:L132, PMC7893703:L28). This adsorption can shift the surface toward more negative values due to the abundance of carboxylic groups in NOM, or, in the case of positively charged particles, adsorption of negatively charged NOM/EPS moieties can create localized 'patch-charge' heterogeneities even without net charge reversal, driving aggregation via patch-charge attraction rather than simple charge neutralization (PMC13057466:L52). Overall, coexisting NOM adsorbs to the particle, forms an eco-corona, and can modulate surface charge (via electrostatic interactions) and DLVO forces, though some studies note that despite confirmed NOM adsorption, zeta potential can remain unchanged, suggesting the effect is not universal or may require other detection methods (PMC13057466:L19, PMC7893703:L30, PMC7893703:L28).", "citations": ["PMC10830523:L132", "PMC7893703:L28", "PMC13057466:L52", "PMC13057466:L19", "PMC7893703:L30"]}

{"answer": "Proteins from serum/plasma adsorb onto the particle surface to form a protein corona, and this adsorbed layer changes the surface charge density of the particle and shields its underlying (e.g., negatively charged) surface, altering the measured zeta potential (PMC4958399:L39, PMC4958399:L42). In TRPS measurements this manifests as a change in particle translocation velocity through the pore—more/higher-affinity protein binding slows translocation and yields a smaller (less negative) zeta potential, while loss of loosely bound soft-corona proteins increases translocation speed and zeta potential (PMC4958399:L49, PMC4958399:L42). The magnitude of the shift depends on which proteins bind, their concentration, affinity, and isoelectric point relative to the solution pH, since proteins adsorbing further from their isoelectric point occupy more surface area and alter charge more strongly (PMC4958399:L39). Similarly, hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions between the plastic surface and albumin can form a hard corona that increases hydrodynamic size and shifts zeta potential due to the added protein layer masking the particle's native charge (PMC12358566:L87)."}

{"answer": "Zeta potential is measured at the particle-liquid shear plane and results from ions in the dispersing medium interacting with the particle's surface functional groups, so it is inherently dependent on the dispersant used (PMC10386368:L45; PMC12590796:L11). When surfactants or salts are added, their molecules or ions adsorb onto the particle surface, and if the surfactant is charged, the particle's surface charge shifts toward the charge of the adsorbed surfactant head groups, which can even reverse the sign of the zeta potential (e.g., CTAB adsorption made polystyrene nanoparticles' zeta potential go from negative to positive) (PMC10734291:L62). Non-ionic surfactants can instead reduce the absolute magnitude of the measured zeta potential by coating the surface and providing steric rather than electrostatic stabilization (PMC10747210:L24; PMC8719689:L36). Additionally, salts/electrolytes in dispersants compress the electrical double layer around particles via counter-ion adsorption, further altering the measured zeta potential (PMC8719689:L36; PMC13488408:L73).", "citations": ["PMC10386368:L45", "PMC12590796:L11", "PMC10734291:L62", "PMC10747210:L24", "PMC8719689:L36", "PMC13488408:L73"]}

{"answer": "UV weathering roughens and fragments the plastic surface and introduces oxygen-containing functional groups, which increases the material's polarity, hydrophilicity, and surface charge (PMC8038232:L19, PMC8038232:L34). These added oxidative groups (e.g., carbonyl and hydroxyl) formed during UV-driven weathering give the particle surface a greater density of ionizable, polar groups that enhance its capacity to interact with polar molecules and increase surface reactivity, shifting the zeta potential to more negative values under neutral/alkaline conditions (PMC8038232:L34, PMC12030786:L119). This is consistent with observations that aged/UV-weathered plastic particles show more negative zeta potentials than pristine particles due to these oxidative surface chemistry changes (PMC12030786:L119).", "citations": ["PMC8038232:L34", "PMC8038232:L19", "PMC12030786:L119"]}
